articleinfo.title: UBL Example Documents: Method and Rationale Version 1.0

abstract.para: This note describes how a coherent set of UBL example documents is created and maintained: a fictional world of organisations that exchange UBL documents with each other, and for every value in every example the reason why it fits the semantic meaning of its element in that context.

legalnotice.title: Notices
legalnotice.para: This is a proposal draft, prepared outside the OASIS UBL Technical Committee. It has not been contributed to, reviewed by or approved by the TC, and it is not an OASIS work product. It may be proposed to the TC as a contribution for a Committee Note.
The layout uses the OASIS DocBook publishing stylesheets (spec-0.9), as used by the OASIS UBL TC. UBL is an OASIS Standard and ISO/IEC 19845.

section.title: Purpose
section.para: UBL defines hundreds of document types and thousands of elements. Its definitions say what an element means, but readers also need to see how an element is used: with which value, in which context, and in relation to the other documents in a business process.

This note describes a method for creating UBL example documents that show exactly that. The examples form one coherent set: they share the same organisations, products and timeline, and documents that belong together refer to each other the way they would in real exchanges.

section.title: Scope
section.para: The method covers:

listitem.para: the fictional world in which the examples take place;
how a value is chosen for an element, and how the reason for that choice is recorded;
how examples are checked, within a document and across documents;
how examples are reviewed and maintained over UBL versions.

section.para: The examples illustrate UBL. They do not define a profile, a customization or a national implementation, and a value used in an example is never the only valid value.

section.title: Starting point
section.para: The example set starts from the sample documents that OASIS published with each UBL 2.x release. Their history, from UBL 2.0 to UBL 2.5, is kept in the repository, one document per commit.

section.title: One fictional UBL world
section.para: All examples take place in the same fictional world: a set of organisations that do all their business with UBL. Documents that belong together, such as a catalogue, an order, a despatch advice and an invoice, or the transport and customs documents for the same goods, tell one consistent story.

section.title: Universal, not tied to one region
section.para: The world includes business within one country, within a region and between continents. No country, legal system or process is the default. Where an example uses a country-specific identifier or rule, it is one illustration among others, not the way UBL has to be used.

section.title: Every value has a reason
section.para: For each element in each example, the reason for its value is recorded: why the value fits the semantic meaning of the element, as defined by UBL, in the context of that document and that business situation. The reason refers to the UBL definition first. Country rules or a specific process only appear as illustrations.

section.title: Proven, not only plausible
section.para: Values are checked automatically:

listitem.para: the document is valid against the UBL schemas and code lists;
the document is consistent in itself, for example totals, dates and internal references;
the documents are consistent with each other, for example parties, references between documents and quantities along a process.

section.title: Open and reproducible
The UBL example world
section.para: All examples take place in one fictional world. It is built in layers. Each layer adds one kind of data, is kept in its own file, and is checked before the next layer builds on it.

row.entry: names, currencies, tax schemes, identifier and address schemes
the organisations: place on the map, role, identity
the flows of documents between the parties
what the parties sell: goods and services, with prices
extracted from the UBL 2.5 semantic model
the world's code lists, and which code element uses which
the transactions, national and community specifications and process profiles the documents claim
the first UBL 2 version of each element, from the published models of UBL 2.0 to 2.5

section.title: Countries
section.para: The world has three countries: Urvania, Bayvarra and Lisavu, whose initials spell UBL. Two share a land border on the mainland; the third is an island overseas. They differ on purpose, so that the examples show how UBL carries different national arrangements in the same structure:

listitem.para: Urvania (XU) has a value added tax in the style of the EU VAT: charged at every stage, deducted by businesses, not charged on exports.
Bayvarra (XB) is a federal country whose states levy a retail sales tax, charged once, on the sale to the final consumer. Sales for resale, exports and sales to public bodies are exempt.
Lisavu (XL) has no general sales tax. Customs collects a customs duty and an import consumption tax when goods enter the island.

section.para: The tax schemes are identified with UN/EDIFACT 5153 codes: VAT, STT (state or provincial sales tax), CUD (customs duty) and IMP (import tax). Because 5153 has no code for a national sales tax, Bayvarra levies its sales tax at state level, which also gives the state in its addresses a purpose. Bayvarra has two states, Upland State inland and Coastal State around Lumeport, and a federal territory, the Northern Territory, on the thinly populated north coast, where the gas plant stands. The territory levies its own rate of the same sales tax: 4 %, against 5 % in Upland State and 6.5 % in Coastal State. Which state a place is in follows from its place on the map.

XU, XB and XL are ISO 3166-1 user-assigned codes, which exist for exactly this purpose; each follows the initial of its country's name. ISO 4217 has no such range for currencies. The world's currencies follow the ISO 4217 convention of the country code plus the initial of the currency's name: the ferra of Urvania (XUF), the lume of Bayvarra (XBL) and the coral of Lisavu (XLC). The convention limits the names: ISO 4217 already uses XUA and XBA to XBD, so Urvania's currency cannot start with an A and Bayvarra's not with A to D. Each code is checked against the current ISO 4217 list, so that none is a real code.

The three currencies also differ in their minor unit, because currencies do: the ferra has none (amounts are whole ferra, as with the Japanese yen), the lume has two decimals, and the coral three (as with the Bahraini or Kuwaiti dinar). An example that only ever shows two decimals hides a case that software must handle. Neither the countries nor the currencies are in the UBL default code lists. UBL lets trading partners use their own code lists in the second phase of validation, so the world has its own: copies of the UBL 2.5 default lists, unchanged, with the world's codes added and their own identification.

In the south-west the land border between Urvania and Bayvarra follows the river: all land south of it is Urvania. The river rises in the hills west of Ferrano and winds east to the sea, widening into an estuary at its mouth below Lumeport. The sawmill stands on its north bank in Upland State, by the water and its forests, as sawmills traditionally do.

The countries also speak differently. Bayvarra speaks English, the working language between the three countries. Urvania was an Italian territory and then under British rule; the British kept the Italian place and street names, while the people kept their own Urvanian names for the same places. Independent since 1962, Urvania is bilingual, Urvanian and English, and the inherited Italian names count as English: Ferrano is also Ruldraz, and an address gives both, as in Brussels. The island is officially bilingual, as many Pacific islands are, in Lisavan and English, Lisavan having a Polynesian sound like the island's names. Both languages are invented, and their codes come from the range ISO 639 reserves for local use, qaa to qtz: qau for Urvanian and qal for Lisavan. A sender from Urvania or the island gives its notes in its own language and in English, each with its languageID, and a seller there names its items in both. Both countries name their streets in both official languages, as Brussels and Canada do: UBL 2.5 lets an address repeat its street, city and state names, one per language; the texts are made word by word from a fixed invented vocabulary, the English text being the reference. Real Polynesian languages are deliberately not used, and the invented words are checked against common words of real languages.

Each country also has an address format (address in world/countries.json), which fixes the lines of an address: first the optional lines (attention, department, in-house mail, post box, building, floor and room), then the street and number (street first in Urvania, number first in Bayvarra and on the island), additional street, block and plot, quarter, and last the town line (postal code before the town in Urvania; the town, state and postal code in Bayvarra), with the province in Urvania and the district and a description of the way on the island. A field the address does not have is left out with its line. A name in two languages is written on its line in both, the national language first, then /, then English, and the number once: <Urvanian street> / <English street> 12 in Urvania, 35 <Lisavan street> / <English street> on the island. Every address that has a street, a building number or a post box carries the code of its country's format in AddressFormatCode, and where a party writes its address in AddressLine elements, one function makes the lines from the structured fields, so they cannot disagree. The build checks all three. A farm on the island has no house number: its track is described instead ("at kilometre 4").

Each country also has its own payment practice, which every invoice of a seller there follows. Urvania gives 2 % discount for payment within ten days and charges statutory interest on late payment; Bayvarra charges a surcharge per month late and rounds cash payments to 5 cents, its smallest coin; the island gives 45 days. A transfer quotes a creditor reference in the structure of ISO 11649, made from the invoice number, so the payee can match it, and runs over the domestic clearing or, between the countries, the trade accord's payment link. Urvania also levies an energy tax per kilowatt hour, in two tiers, on which value added tax is then charged. A public body in Bayvarra withholds 10 % of the price of a service from a business not established there and pays it to the state; such a supplier names a tax representative in Bayvarra. On the island, a buyer of farm produce withholds a presumptive tax, 1 % of a delivery's value up to 2,000 coral and 2 % above, and the farm collects a levy of 1 % for the cotton fund of the chamber of commerce; seed cotton is priced from the trade accord's lint reference price, published in lume. Coral net, the island's clearing, settles tokenised deposits on the Bank of Selanu's ledger. Lumeport's water company also collects the city's sewage levy, as a line collected on behalf of the city, and runs the city's district heating.

Urvania's energy market is unbundled, as the EU's is: a gas-fired power station produces electricity, a grid operator runs the electricity and gas networks and reads the meters, and a retail company buys the energy and bills the customers. The gas comes from an offshore field off Bayvarra's north coast and crosses the border by pipeline. In Bayvarra and on the island one company still does everything, so the three countries show three arrangements.

section.title: Code lists
section.para: Every code in the examples comes from a code list, and every code element names its list in listID. The lists are made from one source, world/codelists/lists.json, as genericode files, together with the world's context/value associations, which say which list each element uses. Where a standard has a list for a concept, the world uses it; otherwise the Lumeport Trade Accord, the treaty between the three countries, has a regional list. A few lists are national, because the countries differ: legal forms, tax exemption reasons, Bayvarra's states and Urvania's customs tariff.

listitem.para: Lists of standards are used where UBL uses them (its default lists), where practice uses them (EN 16931 uses UN/EDIFACT 1001, 5189 and 7161), or where a standard is the authority for its domain: the IMO for emergency schedules and security levels, the WCO for the Harmonized System, the UN for product classification (CPC) and dangerous goods, ISO 20022 for payments, EPSG for coordinates, PRONOM for file formats, UN/ECE Recommendation 28 for means of transport and, as it refers air transport there, IATA's aircraft type codes. UBL is not "EDIFACT in XML", so a UN/EDIFACT list is not used just because it exists. Each is a world copy of the codes the world uses, with others of the same list, made from the copy of the source kept in world/codelists/sources; its listID is in UBL's text style, such as UN/EDIFACT EDED 1001 or WCO HS 2022. No code of such a list is invented.

Regional and national lists have short upper-case codes and a name in English, Urvanian and Lisavan; their listID is a URN such as urn:ubl-examples:world:codelist:AddressTypeCode or urn:ubl-examples:world:XB:codelist:CountrySubentityCode.

One list per concept. Elements that only qualify one concept share its list, as PreviousMeterReadingMethodCode and LatestMeterReadingMethodCode do. An element used for several things, such as TypeCode, gets one list per meaning, chosen by its parent element.
No filler. A code says something the receiver needs. Where "none" matters, it is a defined code, such as UN/EDIFACT 8339 code 4 "Not assigned" for goods without a packing group.

section.para: Some choices differ from common practice, on purpose:

listitem.para: Allowances and charges. An allowance takes its reason from UN/EDIFACT 5189 and a charge from 7161, as in EN 16931. Where 7161 has no code, the world uses 5189 for a charge too, with that list's listID (96 insurance, 48 interest on arrears), which EN 16931 does not allow. UBL's own default list for this element is labelled 5189 but holds the codes of UN/EDIFACT 4465, so the world replaces it.

Languages. Language codes are written in lower case, as ISO 639 and BCP 47 recommend; UBL's copy of the list is in upper case and merges the two alpha-3 codes of a language into one value. The world's list follows the ISO 639-2 registration authority and adds qau and qal. Each sender tags its English texts with its own country as the region, en-XU, en-XB or en-XL, which BCP 47 allows for private use.
Invoice periods. InvoicePeriod/DescriptionCode describes the period (a month), as UBL defines it, not the tax point date code that EN 16931 puts there.

Document distribution. DocumentDistribution/DocumentTypeCode gives the type of the distributed document (a bill of lading), and DistributionTypeCode how the party receives it, original or copy: an original by courier, a scanned copy, the electronic document itself. UBL 2.5 deprecated the elements that said this before (CopyIndicator, MaximumCopiesNumeric, MaximumOriginalsNumeric, PrintQualifier), and an original is not a type of document.

Self-billing. Where the customer bills itself, as the cotton gin does for the farms' seed cotton, the world uses UBL's own SelfBilledInvoice and SelfBilledCreditNote, never an Invoice with type code 389 as EN 16931 and Peppol BIS do (their syntax binding has only Invoice and CreditNote). UBL 2.5 defines Invoice as "A document used to request payment" and SelfBilledInvoice as "An Invoice document created by the Customer (rather than the Supplier) in a Self Billing relationship"; its semantic definitions (§4.7) are what a document must conform to (§7.2). The type codes are UN/EDIFACT 1001 389 and 261: they repeat the root element, but their definitions are exact ("An invoice the invoicee is producing instead of the seller"), while 380 is a document "claiming payment".
Procurement. The Accord's procurement rules are modelled on the EU's, without being EU law: its lists give the matching eForms or ESPD code.

Customs. The Accord is a free trade area, not a customs union: it has one customs data model with common procedures and statuses, while tariffs stay national. A procedure code is the requested procedure followed by the previous one, numbered differently from the EU's, so release for free circulation is 1000.

section.title: Identifiers
section.para: An identifier that comes from a scheme names it in schemeID; one that only its sender assigns, such as a document number or a line number, does not. The world's own schemes have lowercase URNs, as its first ones had (urn:ubl-examples:world:XB:register, urn:ubl-examples:world:endpoint), and a country's scheme carries its code (urn:ubl-examples:world:XU:tax, urn:ubl-examples:world:XB:vehicle-register). Real schemes keep the name their standard gives them, in the text style of UBL's listIDs: ISO 11649 for the creditor references, ISO 6166 for the securities, ISO6346 for the containers. Each scheme has its format in world/countries.json, with its check digit where it has one, and the build checks every identifier against it, as it checks the telephone numbers. A schemeID has no fixed format; the examples show two.

A code held in an identifier element, such as the tax category in TaxCategory/ID, the language in Language/ID, the hazard class or the Incoterms rule in DeliveryTerms/ID, names its code list in schemeID, with the list's listID (UN/EDIFACT EDED 5305, ISO 639), and the world's code list validation checks it like any code. What a dimension or a temperature is (AttributeID) is a code too, from three lists of the Trade Accord: one for dimensions (LENGTH, SEATHEIGHT …), each mapped to the UN/EDIFACT 6313 measured attribute in its description, one for temperatures (STORAGE, PRODUCT, AMBIENT …) and one for the rest (COLOUR, PALLETPLACES, TEU …).

Vehicles are registered nationally: plates, aircraft and railway wagons each have a national scheme. A wagon number follows the UIC's twelve digits with its check digit. Driving licences and identity numbers carry no schemeID: the element already says what they are, and the person's country says whose. Values that would look like real ones are made visibly fictional in the right format: the call signs and aircraft nationality marks use the series QU, QB and QL, which the ITU has not allocated, the ships' MMSIs the unallocated maritime identification digits 297, 298 and 299, and the wagons the UIC country codes 46, 47 and 48, which no railway uses. A container owner code is one the container register of the Bureau International des Containers does not hold, looked up on its public site.

Certificates and licences name their issuer in one of two ways. A number from a national register, such as Urvania's haulage licences and waste permits, Bayvarra's forestry register or its customs' register of bonded warehouses, names the register in schemeID, and with it the authority that keeps it, so no issuer party is needed. A certificate whose number is unique only with its issuer, such as an environmental, medical or sanitation certificate or the X.509 certificate of an access point, has no schemeID and names its issuer in IssuerParty.

Payment cards follow ISO/IEC 7812 in a range real cards cannot use: the major industry identifier 9, which is for national use, followed by the numeric code of the issuer's country (901, 902 and 903 are user-assigned in ISO 3166), the issuer's digits and a Luhn check digit. A chip application starts with its card scheme's application provider identifier from the national category D of ISO/IEC 7816-5 with the same country code. The Accord has three card schemes: Lumecard, the Bayvarran banks' domestic debit card, Coralcard on the island, and Tressa, an international credit card of the banks of all three countries; the names were checked against the real card networks. A till receipt shows the card number as the merchant's till prints it, never more than the first six and the last four digits, and never the card's security code or its dates.

section.title: Parties
section.para: The parties are the organisations of the world, chosen so that every party role in every UBL document type can be filled (see the party cover analysis). Each party has:

listitem.para: a role, such as manufacturer, road carrier or contracting authority;
a place on the map, in a town or a locality;

an identity: a name, the identifiers of its country's schemes, a postal address in its country's format, an electronic address, a contact, and, where it is paid, an account at one of the world's banks;

for a company, its headcount and turnover, from which its size class follows by the Trade Accord's limits, modelled on the EU definition of small and medium-sized enterprises and given in all three currencies.

section.para: Names are invented and checked against real organisations. E-mail addresses use the reserved domain .example (RFC 2606), so that none can reach a real organisation. Telephone numbers use +999, which the ITU reserves for a future global service (ITU-T E.164), followed by the country's digit. Each country has its own numbering plan: Urvania kept the open plan of Italian times, with area codes of different lengths (9 or 10 digits); Bayvarra has a British-style plan of always 10 digits; the island has short 7-digit numbers. Account numbers follow the structure of ISO 13616 with its check digits, using the world's country codes, but they are not called IBANs, because the world's countries are not registered IBAN countries. Each country writes the bank and the branch into the account number in its own way: Bayvarra the bank code and a British-style six-digit sort code, Urvania the Italian-style ABI and CAB codes, the island the bank code and a three-digit branch number. A bank is identified across the countries by a code in the structure of ISO 9362, the BIC, with the world's country codes (BLUMXBLX), which the Trade Accord's payment link gives out, and its branch by the national code; the build checks that every account number holds the codes of its bank and branch.

An address has a number in its country's address register where it is a party's postal address or a delivery address: in Urvania one national register, like the Dutch one, sixteen digits starting with the code of the municipality; in Bayvarra a register per state, except in Lumeport, which keeps the city's own register (LUM-ADR-000417); on the island the post office's numbers of its delivery points, as the island has no postal codes. The build checks that the register is the one of the address's state or city.

section.title: Items
section.para: Every party that sells has items. Goods carry what the documents along their way need: a seller's item identifier, the maker's standard item number where the maker has one (see below), its classification in the UN Central Product Classification (CPC), its Harmonized System subheading and, in Urvania, the national tariff code below it, the country of origin, dimensions, net and gross weight, and the packaging. Services have a unit and a price. Units of measure and packaging types are UN/ECE Recommendation 20 and 21 codes from the UBL default code lists. Prices are in the seller's currency. A unit price may be finer than the currency, as an electricity tariff of 27.3 ferra per kilowatt hour is, but every amount to pay is rounded to the currency's minor unit.

Each party identifies what it makes, ships and runs in one convention, as real companies do. The distributor, the department store and the furniture maker work the GS1 way: a GTIN for their items, a GLN for themselves and their places (the distribution centre's rail siding, the store's goods-in), an SSCC for every pallet or skid they make up. Their company prefixes start with 952, which GS1 reserves for demonstrations and examples. The bench maker, its warehouse, the packaging maker, the power station and the grid operator work the ISO way, through the Codana Identification Agency, which is Urvania's public numbering body: a Codana item number, an organisation identifier in the structure of ISO/IEC 6523 with the code designator 0990, which no real scheme has, and licence plates for their transport units in the structure of ISO/IEC 15459, under the issuing agency code KXU (K is the range for national public administrations, and XU is a user-assigned country code, so no real agency can hold it). The engineering company, the sawmill, the island's cotton farm and ginnery and the utilities use only their own numbers. A reseller shows its own item number and the maker's; where the maker has no GTIN, the GS1 distributor gives the item one of its own, as GS1 allows a wholesaler or importer to do, and the maker's Codana number travels with it. Inner packages have local numbers without a scheme. A logistic unit has the same identifier in every document of its flow, which the build checks.

Items connect the chains. The park bench is made with slats from the sawmill and film from the packaging maker; the distributor resells the bench, and its own item points to the manufacturer's, so the maker's identifiers travel along. A component or a resold item is only possible if the maker or reseller orders it from that seller somewhere in the flows.

The maker's facts travel with the item wherever it appears: brand and model, properties with their test method and accepted range, certificates, the carbon footprint and the circularity profile. What belongs to one delivery is added only where the goods move: a despatch advice names the production lot, or the serial number of every casting, which stays the same when a cancelled despatch advice is replaced. A catalogue line adds the seller's terms (lead time, minimum and maximum quantity, the price list and its validity), and a till receipt during a promotion shows the discount on the shelf price.

section.title: Flows of documents
section.para: The parties do business in flows. Each country has its own raw material and industry: Urvania mines ore and makes park benches, recovering its production waste as recycled plastic; Bayvarra saws timber, makes furniture, packaging and clothing, and distributes and retails; the island Lisavu grows and gins cotton, its export. Goods cross the land border by road, rail and river barge and go overseas by sea and air in both directions; there is a public tender, a temporary export with an ATA carnet, a utility in each country, and gas by pipeline from Bayvarra's offshore field to Urvania's power station and grid. Each flow starts from the business: who buys from whom, on which delivery terms, and therefore who arranges and pays the transport. A distributor that buys free carrier (FCA) books the truck itself and names the carrier in its order; a retailer that buys delivered duty paid (DDP) leaves the transport to its supplier, who then needs an outgoing waybill.
Every document in a flow records:

listitem.para: the document type, its sender and its receiver;
why it is sent, in business terms;
every party it mentions, at its place in the UBL structure, for example the road carrier at Order/Delivery/Despatch/CarrierParty.

section.para: A flow also lists its transport legs: the mode, from which party to which, and the carrier. The goods only move where the world allows it. A road leg needs a road from party to party, so a truck cannot drive to the island; a rail leg needs a rail line between them, a barge needs the river at both ends, gas a pipeline from party to party, a ship a sea route from port to port and an aircraft an air route from airport to airport. The carrier must have a vehicle, train, vessel, aircraft or pipeline of that mode in its fleet, and every carrier a document of the flow names must carry one of its legs. Domestic jobs go to a carrier of that country: a truck of one country driving within another would be cabotage, which only happens where a document says so.

The vehicles on the map are these legs: one truck, train, barge, ship or aircraft per leg, travelling the way the build found for it, from the from-party to the to-party, and a leg flown the same way by the same carrier in several flows is one aircraft. A pipeline has no vehicle: the gas is shown flowing from the field to the consumers. Pipelines follow the rules of real ones. They are buried, so they cross roads, rail lines and the river underneath, at right angles and in a straight line, never along them; they keep out of towns, and nothing is built or planted on their right of way. They start at the producer, at its offshore platform or as a branch of another pipeline, end at a customer, and carry exactly the pipeline legs of the flows, in the direction the gas flows. Where the pipeline crosses the land border, a border metering station measures the gas, as at the interconnection points between real gas networks.

section.title: Specifications
section.para: Every document says which specification it follows. CustomizationID names a transaction: one kind of business message between two roles, with a purpose, a content and rules, as in CEN BII and Peppol. One or more document types carry a transaction (billing is the invoice, the credit note and the debit note), and one document type can carry several (an application response that answers an invoice is not one that answers a message). The specification has up to three levels, chained with #compliant# as EN 16931, Peppol and XRechnung chain theirs: the Trade Accord's transaction (urn:ubl-examples:world:trns:billing:1.0), a national specification built on it, such as Urvania's invoice rules for its value added tax or Bayvarra's rules for bills to its public bodies, and the specification of a community that exchanges among itself: the retail community of the distributor and the store, the port community of Lumeport, Urvania's energy market and public procurement. ProfileID names one of the Accord's generic process profiles (ordering, billing, transport, customs …), versioned, and no longer the flow; ProfileExecutionID still names the run of the process. Each specification has a short public page, and the build checks that every identifier a document uses has one. The world claims no compliance with real specifications such as EN 16931.

UBLVersionID gives the earliest UBL 2 version that defines every element the document uses, as its definition asks. The build computes it from the published models of UBL 2.0 to 2.5. For now every example needs 2.5: nearly all use elements that UBL 2.5 added, such as the electronic address and the further party identification.

section.title: Who sends and who receives
section.para: Who sends and who receives a document type comes from the UBL 2.5 semantic model first: the elements SenderParty and ReceiverParty, or a definition of the document or of one of its party elements, such as "The Party who submits this Tender". Where the model does not say it, the party role table of the UBL specification is used. Where neither says it, the choice is marked as inferred, with the definitions it rests on. Every quote is checked word for word against its source.

section.title: Choosing and documenting values
section.para: Every value in an example document comes with the reason why it is that value. The reason is recorded where the value is made, and a document with a value without a reason is not built.

section.title: Where values come from
section.para: A value in an example comes from one of these sources, and its reason says which:

listitem.para: The world's layers. Party names, addresses, identifiers and accounts come from the identity of the party; items, their identifiers, customs tariff codes and prices from the items layer; currencies and tax rates from the countries layer. These values are the same in every document that uses them.

The structure of the flow. Which party sends the document, which receives it, and which other parties it names, at which place, come from the flow of documents, so the parties always sit where the business puts them.
The scenario of the flow. Document numbers, dates, quantities and the references between documents are what a flow adds; each carries its own reason, in business terms.
Code lists. Coded values come from the UBL default code lists or the world's own lists, and the reason names the list and the meaning of the code.

Calculation. Amounts are calculated from quantities and prices and rounded to the minor unit of the currency; the reason states the calculation. Every sum is stated in the document, as UBL requires, and never left to the receiver.

section.title: What a reason contains
section.para: A reason says why the value fits the element: what the element means in UBL, in this document, and what in the business situation makes this the value. It refers to the UBL definition and to the world's data first; a country rule or a specific process appears only as an illustration. For example, the quantity on an invoice for bulk ore is the weighed quantity from the despatch advice, not the ordered quantity, and its reason says so.

section.title: A party is described once per document
section.para: A party often plays several roles in one document: the buyer of an order is usually also its delivery party. Its full details (address, tax number, legal registration, contact, electronic address) are given once, at its first place in the document. Every later mention of the same party holds only its identifier and its name: enough to identify it, and never empty, as UBL requires (rule IND5). The same applies to a bank named more than once. The identifier is the party's number in its country's company register, given as PartyIdentification with the register as its scheme.

section.title: Only what UBL 2.5 endorses
section.para: The documents use only endorsed document types and elements, and they are validated against the schemas of the endorsed document types. Where UBL 2.5 replaced an element, the examples use the replacement: a party's electronic address, for instance, is carried in ElectronicAddress, because Party/EndpointID is deprecated.

section.title: Kept apart from the TC examples
section.para: The generated examples are kept in world/examples/, apart from the examples of the OASIS UBL Technical Committee in xml/, whose history is the base of this repository.

section.title: Checking the examples
section.para: The world is checked automatically every time the site is built. A build with a problem stops. The checks are layered like the world itself.

section.title: The world against the UBL 2.5 model
section.para: Every document in the world is checked against the UBL 2.5 semantic model:

listitem.para: every place where a party is mentioned exists in the structure of that document type;
every mandatory party element at document level is filled;
every party of the world takes part in at least one document.

section.title: Only what UBL 2.5 endorses
section.para: The examples use only document types, associations and properties that UBL 2.5 endorses. Anything the model marks as deprecated is rejected. A transport service, for example, is invoiced with the Invoice, because the Freight Invoice is deprecated.

section.title: Nothing empty, nothing implied
section.para: Two rules of the UBL specification shape the data the world needs:

listitem.para: No empty elements (IND5). A UBL document never contains an element without content: an aggregate needs a child, a basic element a value, and a value of only spaces counts as empty. Every party element must therefore hold at least one of its parts, even though none of them is mandatory in the schema. The identity of every party makes sure there is always something to put in it.

One text per language (IND7, IND8). Two sibling text elements of the same name never have the same languageID, and never both lack one. A text element repeats only to give the same text in another language, as the bilingual notes do; several keywords of an item therefore go in one search string. The text elements are the basic properties whose data type in the UBL 2.5 model is Text or Name: their schema types derive from the CCTS text type, which carries languageID.
No empty attributes (IND9). Every attribute that is present has a value.

An absence carries no meaning (IND6). Leaving an element out never says anything; the sender states every value that matters, and every sum (section 2.2.2, "Manifest Values"). An order without a carrier does not say that the seller arranges the transport: its delivery terms must say so. The world therefore requires values that would otherwise be implied, such as the delivery terms of every order.

section.title: The parties
section.para: The identity of every party is checked: every party has a name and every organisation an identifier; tax numbers and account numbers carry valid check digits; the city in the address is the nearest town or locality of the party's own country and state; every account is held at a bank of the world in the same country; and a bank named in a document is the bank where that party keeps its account. The ISIN of a listed company has the structure and check digit of ISO 6166 and starts with its country's code.

section.title: The items
section.para: Units and packaging types must be codes of the UBL default lists; world item numbers carry a valid check digit and are unique; prices are positive and in the seller's currency; gross weight is at least net weight. Every party that bills or offers in a document has items to put on its lines, and every party with items bills or offers them. The exchange rates between the currencies agree with each other.

section.title: The map and the code lists
section.para: The map is checked as a structure: one connected road network per landmass, houses on streets, nothing built on roads or water, believable terrain, and customs posts where roads cross a border.

The world's code lists are made from one source, world/codelists/lists.json, and the committed files must be what it makes. The country and currency lists hold exactly the codes of the countries layer. No invented code may be a real one: the currencies are checked against ISO 4217 and the market identifier codes against ISO 10383, both kept in world/codelists/sources. A copy of a real list may hold only codes that its source has.

section.title: The codes in the documents
section.para: The build gives every code its list. A code must be a code of its list, compared exactly, so en is not EN; the element gets the list's listID, and its reason says what the code means in the list. A text next to a code, such as CertificateType beside CertificateTypeCode, carries the list's name for the code. The build also checks what agrees between codes:

listitem.para: every allowance and charge has a reason code;
a tax exemption reason comes from the list of the seller's country;
a payment's clearing channel is one its payment system has, and the service level fits it (decision Q18);

the packing group and the packaging danger level of a UN number agree (I and 1, II and 2, III and 3, NA and 4), the hazardous category is the class, and an emergency card belongs to a class of the goods;
a size class follows from the company's headcount and turnover.

section.title: The example documents
section.para: The build checks that a reference to another document of the same flow quotes that document's UUID wherever it gives one. Every example document is validated in the two phases UBL prescribes:

listitem.para: Phase 1: against the UBL 2.5 runtime schema of its document type, from the endorsed set.

Phase 2: its coded values against the code lists, using context/value associations (CVA). It runs twice. First UBL's own phase 2, unchanged, with the UBL default code lists. The world replaces some of those lists, so this run may object only to values in their contexts: the countries and currencies, the lower-case languages, the allowance and charge codes, and the lists to which the world gives a listID. Then the world's own associations (world/codelists/UBL-World-2.5.cva), which replace UBL's: every code element must carry the listID of its list and a code of that list. An element with several meanings is bound by its parent element; an allowance by its ChargeIndicator (UN/EDIFACT 5189 for an allowance, 7161 or 5189 for a charge); where a context allows several lists, the listID chooses. A code element that no association covers is an error, unless it is a code a party defines for itself. The attributes are checked too: currencyID against the world's currencies, unitCode and mimeCode against UBL's lists, and languageID as a BCP 47 tag, a language of the world's ISO 639 list with an optional region.

section.para: The committed examples must also be up to date: they are generated again from the world's layers and compared, so a change in the world cannot leave an example behind.

section.title: Still to come
section.para: Later layers add their own checks: document lines with items and quantities, amounts and taxes that add up, dates in a believable order, references between documents, and quantities that agree from order to invoice. These apply to the example documents as they are generated for every flow.
